title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (SQL Injection)
content: The software builds an SQL command from user-controllable input without neutralising elements that could alter the command structure. An attacker who controls part of the query can read or modify data beyond their authorisation, and in some configurations execute operating system commands through database features. Typical payload markers include a quote that terminates a literal, a boolean tautology such as OR 1=1, a UNION SELECT that appends attacker-chosen columns, or a comment sequence that truncates the remainder of the statement. The reliable mitigation is parameterised queries or prepared statements, so that user input is always bound as data and never concatenated into the command text. Input validation and stored procedures help but do not substitute for parameterisation, and the database account used by the application should hold only the privileges it needs.

title: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting)
content: The software places user-controllable input into a web page without neutralising it for the output context, allowing script to execute in another user's browser. Variants are reflected, where the payload travels in the request, stored, where it is persisted and served to later visitors, and DOM-based, where client-side code writes untrusted data into the document. Consequences include session token theft, action forgery in the victim's session and defacement. The primary control is context-aware output encoding at the point of rendering, supported by a restrictive Content-Security-Policy and by setting HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies. Common payload markers include script tags, javascript URIs and event handler attributes such as onerror or onload.

title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (OS Command Injection)
content: The software constructs an operating system command from externally influenced input without neutralising shell metacharacters. Successful injection typically yields execution with the privileges of the application process, which is often more than the application itself requires. The preferred mitigation is to avoid the shell entirely by invoking programs with an argument array, and failing that to apply strict allowlisting of permitted values. Semicolons, pipes, backticks and command substitution sequences in a parameter that reaches a command are the characteristic indicators.

title: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (Path Traversal)
content: The software uses external input to construct a pathname without properly neutralising sequences that resolve outside the intended directory. Attackers use relative traversal sequences, sometimes encoded, to read configuration files, credentials or application source. Mitigation is to canonicalise the resolved path and verify that it remains within an approved base directory, rather than filtering traversal strings.

title: Improper Authentication
content: The software does not adequately prove that a claimed identity is correct, allowing an actor to act as another user. Instances include accepting unverified identity assertions, flawed session handling and logic that can be bypassed by manipulating request parameters. Because authentication is the boundary on which authorisation depends, defects here typically have high impact. Mitigation includes using a vetted authentication framework, verifying assertions server side, and adding multi-factor authentication for sensitive access.

title: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
content: The software permits an unlimited or insufficiently limited number of authentication attempts, which makes password guessing and credential stuffing practical. The weakness is the direct enabler of brute-force attacks against an exposed login interface. Mitigations include progressive delays, temporary account lockout, per-source rate limiting and challenge mechanisms after repeated failures. Lockout policy must be balanced against the denial-of-service risk of allowing an attacker to lock legitimate users out deliberately, which is one reason throttling and multi-factor authentication are often preferred to hard lockout.

title: Weak Password Requirements
content: The product does not require users to choose passwords that resist guessing, so credentials fall quickly to dictionary and brute-force attempts. Modern guidance favours a substantial minimum length and screening candidate passwords against lists of known-breached values, rather than mandating composition rules and frequent rotation. Weak password requirements amplify the impact of any missing rate limiting.

title: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
content: The product contains credentials embedded in source code, configuration or firmware. Anyone who can read the artefact obtains the credential, and rotation requires a code change, so the secret tends to persist for years and to be shared across deployments. Mitigation is to load secrets from a managed secret store or environment configuration at runtime, to scan repositories for committed secrets, and to rotate any credential that has ever been committed.

title: Improper Privilege Management
content: The software does not correctly assign, track or revoke privileges, allowing an actor to gain rights beyond those intended. Instances include failing to drop privileges after a privileged operation, granting broad roles by default, and not revoking access when a role changes. Regular entitlement review and least-privilege defaults are the practical mitigations, and any unexplained privilege change should be treated as a potential escalation event.

title: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges
content: The software runs with more privilege than its function requires, so any defect it contains becomes more damaging. Services running as root or as a domain administrator are the classic case. Mitigation is to run each component under a dedicated least-privilege account and to drop elevated rights immediately after any operation that genuinely needs them.

title: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
content: The product discloses information to an actor not explicitly authorised to have it. Disclosure may be direct, such as returning another user's record, or indirect, such as verbose error messages and debug endpoints that reveal internal structure. Exposure often precedes a larger intrusion because it supplies the attacker with the details needed for a targeted attack. Controls include authorisation checks on every retrieval path and suppressing internal detail in error responses.

title: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
content: The software does not encrypt sensitive data in transit or at rest, so anyone with access to the channel or the storage medium can read it. The weakness converts an otherwise limited access event into a full data disclosure. Mitigation is to apply transport encryption for all sensitive traffic and to encrypt sensitive fields or volumes at rest with managed keys.

title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
content: The application performs a state-changing request without verifying that the request was intentionally submitted by the authenticated user. An attacker can therefore cause actions to occur in a victim's session simply by inducing the victim to load a crafted page. Mitigation is to require an unpredictable per-session token on state-changing requests and to set SameSite attributes on session cookies.

title: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
content: The software permits upload of files that can be executed or interpreted by the server environment. When an uploaded file lands in a location that the web server will execute, the result is direct remote code execution. Mitigation is to store uploads outside the web root, to validate type by content rather than extension, to rewrite file names, and to serve uploads from a domain with no execution capability.

title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
content: The software does not properly limit the resources an actor can consume, permitting denial of service with relatively little attacker effort. Unbounded request sizes, unlimited concurrent connections and expensive operations reachable without authentication are common causes. Mitigation is explicit quotas, timeouts and back-pressure at every entry point.

title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
content: The software allocates a reusable resource without limiting how much a single actor may hold, allowing exhaustion of memory, connections, threads or storage. This weakness underlies many application-layer denial-of-service conditions where traffic volume is modest but resource cost per request is high. Mitigation is per-client throttling, connection and memory caps, and rejecting work once a saturation threshold is reached.
